newsitem.title: CHINA: Gulfstream looks to China for business jet sales.
newsitem.headline: Gulfstream looks to China for business jet sales.

text.p: Gulfstream Aerospace Corp has yet to make its first sale to China but it sees this fast- growing economy as a major market for its business jets one day, a senior company official said on Saturday.
"China will be a major market at some time," said Bryan Moss, vice chairman of the U.S.-based maker of business jets.

In a show of confidence, Gulfstream executives made Beijing one of their stops on a world tour of their new corporate jet, the long-range Gulfstream V which boasts a non-stop range of 6,500 nautical miles.
"This pretty well signals Gulfstream's awareness and interest in the China market," Moss told Reuters in an interview.
He gave no firm sales targets and he said some considerable hurdles had to be overcome before market potential could be turned into firm orders.
"There are no Gulfstreams in China now," he said. "Not a lot of people know about Gulfstream let alone business jets."
The Gulfstream V's $35 million to $38 million price tag may be a bit steep in a nation where the bicycle is still the main form of transport for many people.
But China's market-style economic reforms have given financial clout to some of the nation's major companies and swollen foreign currency reserves to $110 billion.
Gulfstream also hopes to convince Beijing that business jets could be used instead of bigger airliners to fly the nation's leaders around the country and abroad.
China's military controls the nation's air space and restricts domestic routes, meaning corporate moguls will not be able to fly around at will in their company jets in the near future.
Fuel and maintenance problems will also hamper sales, Moss said.
By 1999, the company expects to have annual output of 60 business jets, including the Gulfstream IV, which has a range of 4,200 nautical miles. That would double the company's 1995 production level.
Most of Gulfstream's customers are in North America but the rest of the world is expected to account for half of the company's new sales in the years ahead, Moss said.
